reason: The Court construed section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code and held that the 3rd defendant could not be made a plaintiff because no cause of action had accrued to her against the defendants.

The Court's point was that unobjected documents are admitted and routine subject-to-proof objections need not always require witnesses, not that a document marked subject to proof is admissible because there was no objection.
The Court applied a destruction-of-leased-premises test, but the quoted sentence supports only complete destruction and omits the material no-fault/continued-use qualifications.
The quoted sentence is the Court's broad equitable rhetoric, while the operative holding was the narrower availability of possessory relief on proved facts satisfying section 4.
The Court held that the lessors' continuing failure to provide peaceful possession during the lease period barred their claim to rental for that period.
The case did decide that acceptance of a gift may be inferred and may be made on another's behalf, but the selected quote does not support the representative-acceptance and possession/conduct parts.
The proposition was applied, but the supporting quote is expressly from Setha v. Weerakoon and the cited section 545 was not the provision construed for the appellate-new-point rule.

The Court accepted a sham/constructive-trust analysis, but the selected quote supports only sham transfer and the statute attribution to Prevention of Frauds section 2 is not the constructive-trust provision actually applied.
The Court held the transferor had to prove no intention to dispose of beneficial interest under section 83, but the quoted statutory text alone does not state that burden.
The Court held that section 187 requires disclosed reasoning, not numbered answers, where the judgment substantively resolves the points of contest.
The Court applied the co-owner-against-trespasser rule, but the selected quote is from Hevawitarane v. Dangan Rubber Co. Ltd. rather than this Court's own holding.
The Court construed section 4 of the Prescription Ordinance and held that a plaintiff in a possessory action need not prove lawful title.
The quote says a party cannot present a materially different case, and the Court decided the alleged legal impediment was not actually raised for the first time, not the broad rule stated.
The quote records the defendant's contention about occasional use, and the Court rejected the appeal by finding continuous adverse use and a right of way.
The Court held that the writing was a section 6 written promise, but the selected quote is a quotation from Ceylon Insurance rather than this Court's own operative finding.
The Court directly held that acceptance, though not formal or technical as in Roman-Dutch law, is an element for completion of a valid Kandyan-law gift.
The proposition was material to rejecting delay, but the selected quote is from Sirinatha v. Sirisena and not this Court's own statement of the rule.
The statement drops the critical Rent Act and co-owner-consent qualifications and is contrary to the Court's recognition that a valid protected tenancy can survive partition or sale.
The Court ordered a fresh trial because title had not been investigated, but the selected quote about the purpose of partition does not support that rule.
The Court relied on section 5 of the Partition Law to hold that the plaintiff had manifestly disregarded the statutory duty to bring known claimants before Court.
The Court construed section 68 of the Evidence Ordinance and held that a notary may prove execution as an attesting witness if he knew the executant and can identify the signature.
The Court construed section 328 of the Civil Procedure Code and held that possession need not mean physical occupation at the time of execution.
The Court applied the repudiation-of-tenancy principle under section 22, but the selected quote is reproduced from Ranasinghe v. Premadharma rather than this Court's own holding.
The Court applied section 404 to allow substitution after devolution of interest, but the selected quote is from Pless Pol rather than this Court's own reasoning.
The Court held that failure to cite section 83 in the District Court judgment was not fatal absent prejudice, and the quote supports that jurisdiction-validating principle.
